div.head: I Atr Prolog
div.ab: Ðis is seo gerædnys, ðe Æþelred cyning ⁊ his witan geræddon, eallon folce to friþes bote, æt Wudestoce on Myrcena lande, æfter Engla lage.
Ðis is þa geræddnysse, þe Æþelred cining ⁊ his witan geræddon, eallon folce to friþes bote, æt Wudestoce on Myrcena lande, æfter Engla lage.
Hoc est consilium, quod Æþelredus rex et sapientes sui condixerunt, ad emendationem et augmentum pacis omni populo, apud þudestoca in Mircena lande (id est in terra Mircenorum) post Anglie lagam.
Ðis is seo gerædnys þe Æþelred cining ⁊ his witan geræddon, eallon folce to friðes bote, æt Wudestoce on Myrcena lande, æfter Engla lage.
Prolog. Dies ist die Verordnung(en B), welche König Aethelred und seine Witan bestimmten, allem Volke zur Besserung öffentlicher Sicherheit, zu Woodstock im Lande der Mercier, gemäss Engländer-Recht.

Prologue. This is the ordinance (ordinances, B) which King Æthelred and his witan determined, for the improvement of public security for all the people, at Woodstock in the land of the Mercians, according to the law of the English.
This is the ordinance which King Æthelred and his councillors have enacted, at Woodstock in Mercia, for the promotion of public security, wherever English law prevails.

Nicht ‘der Angeln’, da ja Sachsen und Kenter, u. z. an erster Stelle, mitgemeint sind. Der Ggs. ist vielmehr Dena lagu; s. o. Einl. 6; Gl Partikularrecht 3; Engländerrecht 3f.

Not ‘of the Angles’, since Saxons and Kentishmen are of course included as well, and indeed in first place. The contrast is rather Dena lagu; see above Introduction 6; Gl Partikularrecht 3; Engländerrecht 3f.
The plural form in B, in view of the singular verb, is probably incorrect.

Woodstock, a few miles north of Oxford, is described in Domesday Book as a royal forest (see DB. i. 154 b, 2). Oxford, or at least part of it, may have belonged originally to Wessex, but it was in the possession of the Mercians before the great invasion of 866, and may have been annexed by them in the eighth century (see Sax. Chr. ann. 777). In lists of the counties dating from the eleventh and following centuries (see Simeon of Durham, ed. Arnold, Rolls Series, ii., p. 393; Morris, O.E. Miscellany, 1872, p. 146; Gale, Hist. Angl. SS. xv. p. 560) it is represented as belonging to Mercia together with Gloucester, Worcester, Hereford, Warwick, Shropshire, Cheshire, Stafford (cf. Lieb. i. p. 552 f.).
Cf. II Edw. 1; VI As. 8, 4 and 7; 12, 4; II Edm. 5; IV Edg. 2; 12, 1; 14, 1; 15; 16; III Atr. Pre.
The sense seems to involve a local use of the phrase, the districts under English law being contrasted with those under Danish law for which special provisions are made in III Atr.
